cues.text: In Ponferrada, Spain, a man named Juan de Benavente was known in his parish for evident piety, stopping in church each evening to pray.
In 1533, during one such visit, he succumbed to greed and seized the parish tabernacle — a plain wooden box holding a precious silver ciborium filled with consecrated Hosts.
A Tabernacle Too Heavy to Discard
Fleeing toward the Sil River with the stolen tabernacle, Benavente intended to sell the valuable ciborium inside.
He planned to dispose of the evidence in the water, but found the box impossibly, inexplicably heavy when he tried throwing it into the river—far beyond what its actual weight should have allowed.
Unable to fling it into the current as planned, he abandoned it instead in nearby bushes and fled.
In the days that followed, local residents reported flashes of light in the darkness near where the tabernacle had been left.
By day, unusual doves hovered persistently over the same spot, creating a pattern of activity that eventually led searchers to the exact location where Benavente had abandoned his theft.
When the tabernacle was finally recovered, the consecrated Hosts inside were found completely intact and undamaged, despite having been exposed to the elements in a thornbush for an extended period.
The recovery prompted a solemn public procession returning the Sacrament to its parish, the Church of San Pedro.
Like the Herentals and Ettiswil traditions from earlier in this same century, the Ponferrada account centers less on transformation than on simple physical preservation.
It defies every ordinary expectation: the theft was undone not by capture or confession, but by the stolen object's apparent unwillingness to be discarded.
Devotion to the event has continued in Ponferrada for nearly five centuries.
It reminds us that even a devout man's evening habit of prayer proved no guarantee against a single moment's greed.
The story remembered afterward was not his sin but its undoing.
